印卡　*炸雷般地。*您到底在说什么，夫人？印卡的扈从里，您能指出一个不是天生的傻瓜的人吗？
埃明特鲁德　哦，您怎么能这么说！不是有冯·科克皮茨海军上将——
印卡　*不堪忍受地起身，在屋里踱步。*冯·科克皮茨！夫人，冯·科克皮茨若真上了天堂，不出三个礼拜，加百列天使长就得同月亮里那位打起来。
埃明特鲁德　可是冯·申肯堡将军——
印卡　申肯堡！我承认，申肯堡有守菜园的天才。在菜园之间，他战无不胜。可那有什么用？世界并不全由菜园组成。把他放到牧场上，他就完了。

===Original===

The Inca has defeated all these generals again and again at manoeuvres; and yet he has to give place to them in the field because he would be blamed for every disaster﻿—accused of sacrificing the country to his vanity. Vanity! Why do they call him vain? Just because he is one of the few men who are not afraid to live. Why do they call themselves brave? Because they have not sense enough to be afraid to die. Within the last year the world has produced millions of heroes. Has it produced more than one Inca? *He resumes his seat.*
Ermyntrude
Fortunately not, Captain. I’d rather marry Chips.
The Inca
*Making a wry face.* Chips! Oh no: I wouldn’t marry Chips.
Ermyntrude
Why?
The Inca
*Whispering the secret.* Chips talks too much about himself.
Ermyntrude
Well, what about Snooks?
The Inca
Snooks? Who is he? Have I a son named Snooks? There are so many﻿—*wearily* *so* many﻿—that I often forget. *Casually.* But I wouldn’t marry him, anyhow, if I were you.
Ermyntrude
But hasn’t any of them inherited the family genius? Surely, if Providence has entrusted them with the care of Perusalem﻿—if they are all descended from Bedrock the Great﻿—
The Inca
*Interrupting her impatiently.* Madam, if you ask me, I consider Bedrock a grossly overrated monarch.
Ermyntrude
*Shocked.* Oh, Captain! Take care! Incadisparagement.
The Inca
I repeat, grossly overrated. Strictly between ourselves, I do not believe all this about Providence entrusting the care of sixty million human beings to the abilities of Chips and the Piffler and Jack Johnson. I believe in individual genius. That is the Inca’s secret. It must be. Why, hang it all, madam, if it were a mere family matter, the Inca’s uncle would have been as great a man as the Inca. And﻿—well, everybody knows what the Inca’s uncle was.
Ermyntrude
My experience is that the relatives of men of genius are always the greatest duffers imaginable.
The Inca
Precisely. That is what proves that the Inca is a man of genius. His relatives *are* duffers.
Ermyntrude
But bless my soul, Captain, if all the Inca’s generals are incapables, and all his relatives duffers, Perusalem will be beaten in the war; and then it will become a republic, like France after 1871, and the Inca will be sent to St. Helena.
The Inca
*Triumphantly.* That is just what the Inca is playing for, madam. It is why he consented to the war.
Ermyntrude
What!
The Inca
Aha!

===Chinese===

历次演习，印卡把这些将军打得落花流水，一回又一回；可到了战场上，他还得让位于他们，因为一旦有失，什么罪都要算在他头上——说他拿国家喂自己的虚荣。虚荣！他们为什么说他虚荣？就因为他是世上少数几个不怕活着的人。他们为什么自称勇敢？因为他们没有那份脑子来怕死。过去一年，世界造就了千百万英雄。可它造就出第二个印卡了吗？*他回到座位。*
埃明特鲁德　幸亏没有，上尉。我宁可嫁薯片。
印卡　*做了个苦脸。*薯片！哦不：换了我可不嫁薯片。
埃明特鲁德　为什么？
印卡　*耳语这个秘密。*薯片谈自己谈得太多。
埃明特鲁德　那么，斯努克斯怎么样？
印卡　斯努克斯？他是谁？我有叫斯努克斯的儿子吗？儿子太多——*倦然*那么*多*——我常忘记。*随口。*不过换了我，无论如何也不嫁他。
埃明特鲁德　可他们就没有一个承袭了家族的天才？要知道，天意既把佩鲁萨勒姆托付给他们——倘若他们都是“大磐石”的苗裔——
印卡　*不耐烦地打断她。*夫人，您若问我，我认为大磐石是个被大大高估的君主。
埃明特鲁德　*骇然。*哦，上尉！小心！亵渎印卡。
印卡　我再说一遍，大大高估。天知地知你知我知，把六千万人的福祉托付给薯片、废料匠和二代杰克·约翰逊的才干——这一套我是不信的。我相信个人天才。这是印卡的成功秘诀。必然如此。因为，见鬼，夫人，倘若这不过是家门里的事，印卡的叔父就该同印卡一样伟大。而——唉，印卡的叔父是何等人物，谁不知道。
埃明特鲁德　我的经验是，天才的亲属，向来是天底下头一号的笨蛋。
印卡　正是。这恰恰证明印卡是天才。他的亲属*确实*是笨蛋。
埃明特鲁德　可是天哪，上尉，倘若印卡的将军全是庸才，亲属全是笨蛋，佩鲁萨勒姆就要打败仗了；到那时它就会变成共和国，像1871年之后的法国那样，印卡就要被送去圣赫勒拿了。
印卡　*得意洋洋。*印卡图的正是这个，夫人。他之所以应允开战，为的就是它。
埃明特鲁德　什么！
印卡　啊哈！

===Original===

The fools talk of crushing the Inca; but they little know their man. Tell me this. Why did St. Helena extinguish Napoleon?
Ermyntrude
I give it up.
The Inca
Because, madam, with certain rather remarkable qualities, which I should be the last to deny, Napoleon lacked versatility. After all, any fool can be a soldier: we know that only too well in Perusalem, where every fool *is* a soldier. But the Inca has a thousand other resources. He is an architect. Well, St. Helena presents an unlimited field to the architect. He is a painter: need I remind you that St. Helena is still without a National Gallery? He is a composer: Napoleon left no symphonies in St. Helena. Send the Inca to St. Helena, madam, and the world will crowd thither to see his works as they crowd now to Athens to see the Acropolis, to Madrid to see the pictures of Velasquez, to Bayreuth to see the music dramas of that egotistical old rebel Richard Wagner, who ought to have been shot before he was forty, as indeed he very nearly was. Take this from me: hereditary monarchs are played out: the age for men of genius has come: the career is open to the talents: before ten years have elapsed every civilized country from the Carpathians to the Rocky Mountains will be a Republic.
Ermyntrude
Then goodbye to the Inca.
The Inca
On the contrary, madam, the Inca will then have his first real chance. He will be unanimously invited by those Republics to return from his exile and act as Superpresident of all the republics.
Ermyntrude
But won’t that be a comedown for him? Think of it! after being Inca, to be a mere President!
The Inca
Well, why not! An Inca can do nothing. He is tied hand and foot. A constitutional monarch is openly called an India-rubber stamp. An emperor is a puppet. The Inca is not allowed to make a speech: he is compelled to take up a screed of flatulent twaddle written by some noodle of a minister and read it aloud. But look at the American President! He is the *Allerhöchst*, if you like. No, madam, believe me, there is nothing like Democracy, American Democracy. Give the people voting papers: good long voting papers, American fashion; and while the people are reading the voting papers the Government does what it likes.
Ermyntrude
What! You too worship before the statue of Liberty, like the Americans?
The Inca
Not at all, madam. The Americans do not worship the statue of Liberty.

===Chinese===

蠢才们嚷着要打垮印卡；可他们太不了解此人了。我问你。圣赫勒拿为什么熄灭了拿破仑？
埃明特鲁德　我认输。
印卡　因为，夫人，拿破仑固然有些相当了不起的品质——我绝不会否认——却缺少多才多艺。说到底，随便哪个傻瓜都能当兵：这一点佩鲁萨勒姆再清楚不过，那儿每个傻瓜*都*是兵。可印卡另有一千种本领。他是建筑师。好啊，圣赫勒拿给建筑师提供了无限的天地。他是画家：还用我提醒您吗，圣赫勒拿到如今还没有一座国家美术馆？他是作曲家：拿破仑在圣赫勒拿可没留下交响曲。把印卡送去圣赫勒拿吧，夫人，世人会蜂拥去看他的作品，就像如今蜂拥去雅典看卫城、去马德里看委拉斯开兹的画、去拜罗伊特看那个自我中心的老叛徒理查德·瓦格纳的乐剧——那家伙本该四十岁前枪毙的，事实上也差点儿挨了枪毙。记住我这句话：世袭君主过时了：天才的时代到来了：前程向才能敞开：不出十年，从喀尔巴阡山到落基山，每一个文明国家都将是共和国。
埃明特鲁德　那印卡就再见了。
印卡　恰恰相反，夫人，届时印卡将得到他第一个真正的机会。那些共和国将一致邀请他结束流亡归来，出任全联盟超级大总统。
埃明特鲁德　可那对他不是降格吗？想想！做过印卡，再屈尊做个区区总统！
印卡　嗐，为什么不！印卡什么都做不成。他手足都被捆着。立宪君主被公开叫作橡皮图章。皇帝是个傀儡。印卡连演说都不许：他只能拿起某位面条大臣写的一篇浮夸废话，高声宣读。可瞧瞧美国总统！那才是*至高者*，如您所愿。不，夫人，相信我，什么都比不上民主，美国式民主。给人民选票：长长的选票，美国样式；人民读选票的当口，政府爱干什么干什么。
埃明特鲁德　什么！您也拜倒在自由女神像前，跟美国人一样？
印卡　才不呢，夫人。美国人并不崇拜自由女神像。

===Original===

They have erected it in the proper place for a statue of Liberty: on its tomb. *He turns down his moustaches.*
Ermyntrude
*Laughing.* Oh! You’d better not let them hear you say that, Captain.
The Inca
Quite safe, madam: they would take it as a joke. *He rises.* And now, prepare yourself for a surprise. *She rises.* A shock. Brace yourself. Steel yourself. And do not be afraid.
Ermyntrude
Whatever on earth can you be going to tell me, Captain?
The Inca
Madam, I am no captain. I﻿—
Ermyntrude
You are the Inca in disguise.
The Inca
Good heavens! how do you know that? Who has betrayed me?
Ermyntrude
How could I help divining it, Sir? Who is there in the world like you? Your magnetism﻿—
The Inca
True: I had forgotten my magnetism. But you know now that beneath the trappings of Imperial Majesty there is a Man: simple, frank, modest, unaffected, colloquial: a sincere friend, a natural human being, a genial comrade, one eminently calculated to make a woman happy. You, on the other hand, are the most charming woman I have ever met. Your conversation is wonderful. I have sat here almost in silence, listening to your shrewd and penetrating account of my character, my motives, if I may say so, my talents. Never has such justice been done me: never have I experienced such perfect sympathy. Will you﻿—I hardly know how to put this﻿—will you be mine?
Ermyntrude
Oh, Sir, you are married.
The Inca
I am prepared to embrace the Muhammadan faith, which allows a man four wives, if you will consent. It will please the Turks. But I had rather you did not mention it to the Inca-ess. If you don’t mind.
Ermyntrude
This is really charming of you. But the time has come for me to make a revelation. It is your Imperial Majesty’s turn now to brace yourself. To steel yourself. I am not the princess. I am﻿—
The Inca
The daughter of my old friend Archdeacon Daffodil Donkin, whose sermons are read to me every evening after dinner. I never forget a face.
Ermyntrude
You knew all along!
The Inca
*Bitterly, throwing himself into his chair.* And you supposed that I, who have been condemned to the society of princesses all my wretched life, believed for a moment that any princess that ever walked could have your intelligence!
Ermyntrude
How clever of you, Sir! But you cannot afford to marry me.
The Inca
*Springing up.* Why not?
Ermyntrude
You are too poor. You have to eat war bread.

===Chinese===

他们把像立在了自由神像该立的地方：立在它的坟墓上。*他把胡子捻下去。*
埃明特鲁德　*大笑。*哦！这话可别叫他们听见，上尉。
印卡　安全得很，夫人：他们会当这是玩笑。*他起身。*现在，请准备接受一个意外。*她起身。*一个震动。站稳了。撑住。别怕。

印卡　夫人，我不是什么上尉。我——
埃明特鲁德　您是微服的印卡。
印卡　天哪！您怎么知道？谁出卖了我？
埃明特鲁德　我怎么会猜不出呢，陛下？世上还有第二个您这样的人吗？您的磁力——
印卡　是了：我忘了我的磁力。可您如今知道了，在帝王威仪的行头底下，有一个人：朴实、坦率、谦逊、不做作、如话家常：一位真挚的朋友，一个本色的人，一位和气的同志，一个天造地设能给女人幸福的人。而您呢，是我平生所见最迷人的女子。您的谈吐妙不可言。我坐在这里几乎一言不发，听您锐利而透辟地剖析我的品格、我的动机——恕我僭妄——还有我的才具。从未有人如此公道地待我：从未有人给我这般完满的知音之感。您可愿——这话我几乎不知从何说起——您可愿属于我？
埃明特鲁德　哦，陛下，您是有妇之夫。
印卡　您若肯允，我准备皈依穆罕默德教门，那教门许男人四位妻室。这会讨土耳其人喜欢。不过这件事，您最好别向印卡后提起。若您不介意。
埃明特鲁德　您这可真是叫人心醉。不过，如今轮到我揭开一桩底细了。这回要站稳的，是陛下您了。要撑住的，是您了。我不是公主。我是——
印卡　我老友水仙花·唐金会吏总的千金——他那些布道文，每天晚饭后都有人念给我听。我过目不忘。
埃明特鲁德　您早就知道了！
印卡　*痛心地跌进椅子。*您竟以为，我这个苦命人，一辈子被判在公主堆里厮混，会有一刻相信，天底下随便哪位公主，能有您这样的智力！
埃明特鲁德　您真高明，陛下！可您娶不起我。
印卡　*跳起来。*为什么？
埃明特鲁德　您太穷了。您吃的是战时面包。

===Original===

Kings nowadays belong to the poorer classes. The King of England does not even allow himself wine at dinner.
The Inca
*Delighted.* Haw! Ha ha! Haw! haw! *He is convulsed with laughter, and, finally has to relieve his feelings by waltzing half round the room.*
Ermyntrude
You may laugh, Sir; but I really could not live in that style. I am the widow of a millionaire, ruined by your little war.
The Inca
A millionaire! What are millionaires now, with the world crumbling?
Ermyntrude
Excuse me: mine was a hyphenated millionaire.
The Inca
A highfalutin millionaire, you mean. *Chuckling.* Haw! ha ha! really very nearly a pun, that. *He sits down in her chair.*
Ermyntrude
*Revolted, sinking into his chair.* I think it quite the worst pun I ever heard.
The Inca
The best puns have all been made years ago: nothing remained but to achieve the worst. However, madam *he rises majestically; and she is about to rise also.* No: I prefer a seated audience. *She falls back into her seat at the imperious wave of his hand.* So. *He clicks his heels.* Madam, I recognize my presumption in having sought the honor of your hand. As you say, I cannot afford it. Victorious as I am, I am hopelessly bankrupt; and the worst of it is, I am intelligent enough to know it. And I shall be beaten in consequence, because my most implacable enemy, though only a few months further away from bankruptcy than myself, has not a ray of intelligence, and will go on fighting until civilization is destroyed, unless I, out of sheer pity for the world, condescend to capitulate.
Ermyntrude
The sooner the better, Sir. Many fine young men are dying while you wait.
The Inca
*Flinching painfully.* Why? Why do they do it?
Ermyntrude
Because you make them.
The Inca
Stuff! How can I? I am only one man; and they are millions. Do you suppose they would really kill each other if they didn’t want to, merely for the sake of my beautiful eyes? Do not be deceived by newspaper claptrap, madam. I was swept away by a passion not my own, which imposed itself on me. By myself I am nothing. I dare not walk down the principal street of my own capital in a coat two years old, though the sweeper of that street can wear one ten years old. You talk of death as an unpopular thing.

如今的国王都属于穷苦阶级。英格兰国王连晚饭都不许自己喝酒。

埃明特鲁德　越早越好，陛下。您迟疑的每一天，都有多少好青年在死去。

埃明特鲁德　因为您叫他们这么做。

===Original===

You are wrong: for years I gave them art, literature, science, prosperity, that they might live more abundantly; and they hated me, ridiculed me, caricatured me. Now that I give them death in its frightfullest forms, they are devoted to me. If you doubt me, ask those who for years have begged our taxpayers in vain for a few paltry thousands to spend on Life: on the bodies and minds of the nation’s children, on the beauty and healthfulness of its cities, on the honor and comfort of its worn-out workers. They refused; and because they refused, death is let loose on them. They grudged a few hundreds a year for their salvation: they now pay millions a day for their own destruction and damnation. And this they call my doing! Let them say it, if they dare, before the judgment-seat at which they and I shall answer at last for what we have left undone no less than for what we have done. *Pulling himself together suddenly.* Madam, I have the honor to be your most obedient. *He clicks his heels and bows.*
Ermyntrude
Sir! *She curtsies.*
The Inca
*Turning at the door.* Oh, by the way, there is a princess, isn’t there, somewhere on the premises?
Ermyntrude
There is. Shall I fetch her?
The Inca
*Dubious.* Pretty awful, I suppose, eh?
Ermyntrude
About the usual thing.
The Inca
*Sighing.* Ah well! What can one expect? I don’t think I need trouble her personally. Will you explain to her about the boys?
Ermyntrude
I am afraid the explanation will fall rather flat without your magnetism.
The Inca
*Returning to her and speaking very humanly.* You are making fun of me. Why does everybody make fun of me? Is it fair?
Ermyntrude
*Seriously.* Yes, it is fair. What other defence have we poor common people against your shining armor, your mailed fist, your pomp and parade, your terrible power over us? Are these things fair?
The Inca
Ah, well, perhaps, perhaps. *He looks at his watch.* By the way, there is time for a drive round the town and a cup of tea at the Zoo. Quite a bearable band there: it does not play any patriotic airs. I am sorry you will not listen to any more permanent arrangement; but if you would care to come﻿—
Ermyntrude
*Eagerly.* Ratherrrrrr. I shall be delighted.
The Inca
*Cautiously.* In the strictest honor, you understand.
Ermyntrude
Don’t be afraid. I promise to refuse any incorrect proposals.
The Inca
*Enchanted.* Oh!

===Chinese===

您错了：多年来我给他们艺术、文学、科学、繁荣，好教他们活得更丰盈；他们恨我，讥我，把我画成漫画。如今我给他们最狰狞形态的死亡，他们倒对我忠心耿耿。您若不信，去问问那些人：他们多年苦苦哀求纳税人，讨几千个区区小数，花在生命上：花在国民儿童的身心上，花在城市的美丽与健康上，花在筋疲力尽的劳动者的体面与安逸上，却始终徒劳。他们拒绝了；正因他们拒绝，死亡才放出来咬他们。为自己的得救，他们一年几百块都吝惜；如今为自己的毁灭与沉沦，他们一天付千百万。而这，他们竟说是我干的！让他们去说吧，若他们敢，到那座审判席前说去——在那席前，他们和我，终须为我们做过的事答辩，同样也为我们没做的事答辩。*猛然收摄心神。*夫人，恕我做您最恭顺的仆人。*他碰响脚跟，一躬到底。*
埃明特鲁德　陛下！*她行屈膝礼。*
印卡　*在门口回身。*哦，对了，这宅子里某处，还有位公主，是吧？
埃明特鲁德　在。要我去叫她吗？
印卡　*迟疑。*相当吓人吧，嗯？
埃明特鲁德　照例的水平。
印卡　*叹气。*唉，也罢！还能指望什么呢？我看不必亲自烦劳她了。诸位公子的事，由您向她解释一下，可好？
埃明特鲁德　只怕没有您的磁力，这番解释要平淡无味了。

埃明特鲁德　*正色。*公道。我们这些可怜的平民，面对您闪亮的甲胄、您的铁拳、您的排场与仪仗、您加于我们的可怕权力，除了取笑，还有什么傍身之器？那些东西又公道吗？

## Endnotes / 尾注
===Original===

1. In a treatise on boxing by Captain Edgeworth Johnstone, just published, I read, “In the days of the prize-ring, fights lasted for hours; and the knockout blow was unknown.” This statement is a little too sweeping. The blow was known well enough. A veteran prizefighter once described to me his first experience of its curious effect on the senses. Only, as he had thirty seconds to recover in instead of ten, it did not end the battle. The thirty seconds made the knockout so unlikely that the old pugilists regarded it as a rare accident, not worth trying for. The glove fighter tries for nothing else. Nevertheless knockouts, and very dramatic ones too (Mace by King, for example), did occur in the prize-ring from time to time. Captain Edgeworth Johnstone’s treatise is noteworthy in comparison with the earlier Badminton handbook of sparring by Mr. E. B. Michell (one of the Queensberry champions) as throwing over the old teaching of prize-ring boxing with mufflers, and going in frankly for glove fighting, or, to put it classically, cestus boxing. ↩︎

===Chinese===

1. 在刚出版的埃奇沃思·约翰斯通上尉的拳击论著里，我读到：“在拳击场的年代，一场打斗可持续几个钟头；击倒一击则无人知晓。”这话稍稍说得太满。这一击是人人皆知的。一位老职业拳手曾向我描述他头一回领教它对感官的奇妙作用。只不过，那时他有三十秒而不是十秒恢复，所以一击并不终结战斗。那三十秒使击倒变得如此难得，以致老拳师们把它看作帘见的意外，不值得特意去求。而戴拳套的拳手所求的别无其他。尽管如此，拳击场年代也确实不时出现击倒，而且颇具戏剧性（如金击倒梅斯一例）。埃奇沃思·约翰斯通上尉的论著之所以值得注意，在于同早先 E.B.米切尔先生（昆斯伯里规则时代的冠军之一）那本巴德明顿拳击手册相比，它抛弃了戴护具的拳击场旧法，坦率地转向拳套格斗——用古典的话说，即皮质拳击。 ↩︎

## Great Catherine / 伟大的凯瑟琳
===Original===

> “In Catherine’s reign, whom Glory still adores”
> — Byron

===Chinese===

> “在凯瑟琳的时代，荣光至今仍崇拜她”
> ——拜伦

### The Author’s Apology for “Great Catherine” / 作者为《伟大的凯瑟琳》一辩

### The Author’s Apology for “Great Catherine” /

### The Author’s Apology for “Great Catherine” /

### The Author’s Apology for “Great Catherine” /

### The Author’s Apology for “Great Catherine” /

### The Author’s Apology for “Great Catherine” /

### The Author’s Apology for “Great Catherine” / 
===Original===

Exception has been taken to the title of this seeming tomfoolery on the ground that the Catherine it represents is not Great Catherine, but the Catherine whose gallantries provide some of the lightest pages of modern history. Great Catherine, it is said, was the Catherine whose diplomacy, whose campaigns and conquests, whose plans of Liberal reform, whose correspondence with Grimm and Voltaire enabled her to cut such a magnificent figure in the eighteenth century. In reply, I can only confess that Catherine’s diplomacy and her conquests do not interest me. It is clear to me that neither she nor the statesmen with whom she played this mischievous kind of political chess had any notion of the real history of their own times, or of the real forces that were moulding Europe. The French Revolution, which made such short work of Catherine’s Voltairean principles, surprised and scandalized her as much as it surprised and scandalized any provincial governess in the French châteaux.
The main difference between her and our modern Liberal Governments was that whereas she talked and wrote quite intelligently about Liberal principles before she was frightened into making such talking and writing a flogging matter, our Liberal ministers take the name of Liberalism in vain without knowing or caring enough about its meaning even to talk and scribble about it, and pass their flogging Bills, and institute their prosecutions for sedition and blasphemy and so forth, without the faintest suspicion that such proceedings need any apology from the Liberal point of view.
It was quite easy for Patiomkin to humbug Catherine as to the condition of Russia by conducting her through sham cities run up for the occasion by scenic artists; but in the little world of European court intrigue and dynastic diplomacy which was the only world she knew she was more than a match for him and for all the rest of her contemporaries. In such intrigue and diplomacy, however, there was no romance, no scientific political interest, nothing that a sane mind can now retain even if it can be persuaded to waste time in reading it up. But Catherine as a woman with plenty of character and (as we should say) no morals, still fascinates and amuses us as she fascinated and amused her contemporaries.

===Chinese===

有人对这篇看似胡闹的东西的题目提出异议，说它写的凯瑟琳不是伟大的凯瑟琳，而是那位以其艳史为近代史添了几页最轻快的文字的凯瑟琳。据说，伟大的凯瑟琳，是那位以她的外交、她的征战与征服、她的自由主义改革计划、她同格里姆和伏尔泰的通信，在十八世纪里活得那样辉煌的凯瑟琳。作为回答，我只能承认：凯瑟琳的外交和征服，我不感兴趣。我看得分明，无论是她，还是同她下这种为害甚烈的政治棋的各国政治家，对他们自己时代的真实历史、对雕塑着欧洲的真正力量，都毫无概念。法国大革命把凯瑟琳那套伏尔泰式原则三下五除二扫了个精光，它的突兀和丑闻，之叫她吃惊，正如叫法国城堡里任何一个外省女塾师吃惊一样。
她同我们近代自由党政府的主要分别在于：她曾在被吓得以谈论和写作此道为鞭刑之罪以前，把自由主义原则谈得、写得相当聪明；而我们的自由党大臣们，盗用自由主义之名，既不知也不属其义，连谈一谈、涂一涂都不屑，一面通过他们的鞭刑法案，一面就煽动、渎神等等提起公诉，丝毫没有想到这类行径从自由主义的立场看还需要任何道歉。
帕乔姆金可以借布景师们赶造的假城市领着凯瑟琳巡游，骗过她俄罗斯的状况；可是在欧洲宫廷阴谋与王朝外交那个小天地里——那是她知道的唯一天地——她胜过他，也胜过她所有的同代人。然而那样的阴谋与外交里，没有浪漫，没有科学的政治兴味，没有一个健全的头脑如今肯保留的东西，哪怕被劝动白费时间去研读。可是凯瑟琳作为女人，性格十足而（照我们的说法）毫无道德，至今仍像当年迷住、逗乐她的同代人一样，迷住、逗乐着我们。

===Original===

They were great sentimental comedians, these Peters, Elizabeths, and Catherines who played their Tsarships as eccentric character parts, and produced scene after scene of furious harlequinade with the monarch as clown, and of tragic relief in the torture chamber with the monarch as pantomime demon committing real atrocities, not forgetting the indispensable love interest on an enormous and utterly indecorous scale. Catherine kept this vast Guignol Theatre open for nearly half a century, not as a Russian, but as a highly domesticated German lady whose household routine was not at all so unlike that of Queen Victoria as might be expected from the difference in their notions of propriety in sexual relations.
In short, if Byron leaves you with an impression that he said very little about Catherine, and that little not what was best worth saying, I beg to correct your impression by assuring you that what Byron said was all there really is to say that is worth saying. His Catherine is my Catherine and everybody’s Catherine. The young man who gains her favor is a Spanish nobleman in his version. I have made him an English country gentleman, who gets out of his rather dangerous scrape by simplicity, sincerity, and the courage of these qualities. By this I have given some offence to the many Britons who see themselves as heroes: what they mean by heroes being theatrical snobs of superhuman pretensions which, though quite groundless, are admitted with awe by the rest of the human race. They say I think an Englishman a fool. When I do, they have themselves to thank.
I must not, however, pretend that historical portraiture was the motive of a play that will leave the reader as ignorant of Russian history as he may be now before he has turned the page. Nor is the sketch of Catherine complete even idiosyncratically, leaving her politics out of the question. For example, she wrote bushels of plays. I confess I have not yet read any of them. The truth is, this play grew out of the relations which inevitably exist in the theatre between authors and actors. If the actors have sometimes to use their skill as the author’s puppets rather than in full self-expression, the author has sometimes to use his skill as the actors’ tailor, fitting them with parts written to display the virtuosity of the performer rather than to solve problems of life, character, or history.

===Chinese===

他们是一些伟大的感伤喜剧演员，这些彼得、伊丽莎白和凯瑟琳，把他们的沙皇之位演成古怪的性格角色，一幕接一幕：君主扮丑角的狂暴滑稽，还有 torture chamber→刑房里以君主扮哑剧恶魔、干出真实暴行的惨烈的松缓，更不消说那必不可少的、规模浩大而全然不得体的爱情穿插。凯瑟琳把这座宏大的木偶剧场开了将近半个世纪；她开剧场不是以俄国人的身份，而是以一位极居家的德国夫人的身份，其家常的作息，同维多利亚女王的并不像两人两性贞操观念的悬殊所叫人意料的那样不同。
总之，倘若拜伦留给你的印象是：关于凯瑟琳他说得很少，而且那很少的也未必是最值得说的，那我请你更正：拜伦所说的，就是一切值得说的话的全部。他的凯瑟琳就是我的凯瑟琳，也是人人的凯瑟琳。在他笔下，博得她欢心的青年是一位西班牙贵族。我把他改成了一位英国乡绅，靠纯朴、真诚，靠这两种品质带来的勇气，脱身于那相当危险的窘境。此举触怒了不少把自己看作英雄的英国人：他们所谓英雄，是那种戏剧性的、自命超人的势利眼——毫无根据，却被其余人类敬畏地默认。他们说我把英国人当傻瓜。我何时当真，他们该谢自己。
不过我不能佯称，历史画像就是这出戏的动机；读完此戏，读者对俄国史的了解，同翻页之前一样无知。这幅凯瑟琳的素描，即便只论其人而不论其政，也不完整。譬如，她写过成清式耳的戏。我承认我一部也没读过。实情是，这出戏长自剧场上作者与演员之间必然存在的关系。演员有时不得不把自己的技艺当作者的傀儡使，而非充分的自我表现；作者有时也不得不把自己的技艺当演员的裁缝，为他们裁写旨在展示演员绝技的戏，而非解决人生、性格或历史的问题。

===Original===

Feats of this kind may tickle an author’s technical vanity; but he is bound on such occasions to admit that the performer for whom he writes is “the onlie begetter” of his work, which must be regarded critically as an addition to the debt dramatic literature owes to the art of acting and its exponents. Those who have seen Miss Gertrude Kingston play the part of Catherine will have no difficulty in believing that it was her talent rather than mine that brought the play into existence. I once recommended Miss Kingston professionally to play queens. Now in the modern drama there were no queens for her to play; and as to the older literature of our stage, did it not provoke the veteran actress in Sir Arthur Pinero’s *Trelawny of the Wells* to declare that, as parts, queens are not worth a tinker’s oath? Miss Kingston’s comment on my suggestion, though more elegantly worded, was to the same effect; and it ended in my having to make good my advice by writing “Great Catherine.” History provided no other queen capable of standing up to our joint talents.
In composing such bravura pieces, the author limits himself only by the range of the virtuoso, which by definition far transcends the modesty of nature. If my Russians seem more Muscovite than any Russian, and my English people more insular than any Briton, I will not plead, as I honestly might, that the fiction has yet to be written that can exaggerate the reality of such subjects; that the apparently outrageous Patiomkin is but a timidly bowdlerized ghost of the original; and that Captain Edstaston is no more than a miniature that might hang appropriately on the walls of nineteen out of twenty English country houses to this day. An artistic presentment must not condescend to justify itself by a comparison with crude nature; and I prefer to admit that in this kind my dramatis personae are, as they should be, of the stage stagey, challenging the actor to act up to them or beyond them, if he can. The more heroic the overcharging, the better for the performance.

===Chinese===

这一类的绝技可以撩拨作者的技术虚案；可在这种场合他必须承认：他为之写作的那位表演家才是他作品“独一无二的孕育者”；从批评的眼光看，这作品须算戏剧文学欠表演艺术及其代表人物的又一笔债。凡看过格特鲁德·金斯顿小姐演凯瑟琳的人，都不难相信：使这出戏得以降生的，是她的才华，不是我的。我曾以行家身份劝金斯顿小姐演女王。可现代戏剧里没有女王可演；至于我们舞台的老剧目，阿瑟·皮尼罗爵士的《特雷洛尼的温泉》里那位老演员娘子不是发过牢骚，说女王这种角色一文不值吗？金斯顿小姐对我这建议的回话，措辞虽更雅，意思相同；结果是我只好用写出《伟大的凯瑟琳》来兑现我的忠告。历史上再找不出第二位顶得住我们俩联手才华的女王。
写这一类华彩段子，作者给自己设的唯一界限，就是这位高手的能力范围，而那范围照定义远超自然的本分。倘若我笔下的俄国人比任何俄国人更像俄国人，我笔下的英国人比任何英国人更岛气，我不打算老老实实辩一句：写这类题材再夸张也超不过现实的小说还没出世；那个看似骇人听闻的帕乔姆金，不过是原版一个小心消毒过的幽灵；而埃德斯塔斯顿上尉，不过是一幅缩像，至今还合宜地挂得上二十座英国乡宅里十九座的墙。艺术的表现，不该降尊纡贵，靠同比相自然来给自己辩护；我宁愿承认：在这个品类里，我的人物像理应的那样，戏味十足，向演员发出战书，要他演到他们，或者演到他们之上——只要他行。超额装得越英雄，演出就越好看。

===Original===

In dragging the reader thus for a moment behind the scenes, I am departing from a rule which I have hitherto imposed on myself so rigidly that I never permit myself, even in a stage direction, to let slip a word that could bludgeon the imagination of the reader by reminding him of the boards and the footlights and the sky borders and the rest of the theatrical scaffolding, for which nevertheless I have to plan as carefully as if I were the head carpenter as well as the author. But even at the risk of talking shop, an honest playwright should take at least one opportunity of acknowledging that his art is not only limited by the art of the actor, but often stimulated and developed by it. No sane and skilled author writes plays that present impossibilities to the actor or to the stage engineer. If, as occasionally happens, he asks them to do things that they have never done before and cannot conceive as presentable or possible (as Wagner and Thomas Hardy have done, for example), it is always found that the difficulties are not really insuperable, the author having foreseen unsuspected possibilities both in the actor and in the audience, whose will-to-make-believe can perform the quaintest miracles. Thus may authors advance the arts of acting and of staging plays. But the actor also may enlarge the scope of the drama by displaying powers not previously discovered by the author. If the best available actors are only Horatios, the authors will have to leave Hamlet out, and be content with Horatios for heroes. Some of the difference between Shakespeare’s Orlandos and Bassanios and Bertrams and his Hamlets and Macbeths must have been due not only to his development as a dramatic poet, but to the development of Burbage as an actor. Playwrights do not write for ideal actors when their livelihood is at stake: if they did, they would write parts for heroes with twenty arms like an Indian god. Indeed the actor often influences the author too much; for I can remember a time (I am not implying that it is yet wholly past) when the art of writing a fashionable play had become very largely the art of writing it “round” the personalities of a group of fashionable performers of whom Burbage would certainly have said that their parts needed no acting. Everything has its abuse as well as its use.

===Chinese===

这样把读者拽到后台一瞬，我违背了一条自己至今守得极严的规矩：哪怕在舞台提示里，我也不许自己走漏一个字，去提醒他木板、脚灯、天幕和其余的剧场脚手架，从而钝击他的想象——尽管这一切我又必须像总木匠兼作者那样精心筹划。可是哪怕犯谈本行，一个诚实的剧作家也该至少捉住一次机会承认：他的艺术不仅受演员艺术的限制，也常常被它激发、被它发扬。没有一个神志清醒、技艺娴熟的作者，会写出令演员或舞台工程师绝无可能实现的戏。倘若——这偶有发生——他要求他们做他们从未做过、且无法想象如何呈现或如何可行的事（如瓦格纳和托马斯·哈代就干过），到头来总会发现困难并非真的不可逾越，因为作者在演员身上和在观众身上预见到了不曾料到的可能，观众的姑妄信之能演出最古怪的奇迹。作者由此可以推动表演与舞台装置的艺术。但演员也可以发挥出作者未先发现的才能，从而拓宽戏剧的疆域。倘若当时最好的演员只演得了霍拉旭，作者们就只好舍弃哈姆雷特，拿霍拉旭当英雄。莎士比亚的奥兰多、巴萨尼奥、伯特伦，同他的哈姆雷特、麦克白之间的某些差别，必然不仅缘于他作为戏剧诗人的成长，也缘于伯比奇作为演员的成长。剧作家在生计攸关时，不为理想的演员写戏：真为理想的演员写，他们会给英雄写上二十条胳膊，像印度神一样。其实演员对作者的影响倒往往过了头；我记得有过那样一个时代（我并不是说它已全然过去）：写时兴戏的艺术，很大程度上成了围绕一班时兴名角儿的个性来写的艺术——伯比奇若见了那班人，肯定会说他们的角色用不着演。凡事有用即有其弊。

===Original===

It is also to be considered that great plays live longer than great actors, though little plays do not live nearly so long as the worst of their exponents. The consequence is that the great actor, instead of putting pressure on contemporary authors to supply him with heroic parts, falls back on the Shakespearean repertory, and takes what he needs from a dead hand. In the nineteenth century, the careers of Kean, Macready, Barry Sullivan, and Irving, ought to have produced a group of heroic plays comparable in intensity to those of Aeschylus, Sophocles, and Euripides; but nothing of the kind happened: these actors played the works of dead authors, or, very occasionally, of live poets who were hardly regular professional playwrights. Sheridan Knowles, Bulwer Lytton, Wills, and Tennyson produced a few glaringly artificial high horses for the great actors of their time; but the playwrights proper, who really kept the theatre going, and were kept going by the theatre, did not cater for the great actors: they could not afford to compete with a bard who was not for an age but for all time, and who had, moreover, the overwhelming attraction for the actor-managers of not charging author’s fees. The result was that the playwrights and the great actors ceased to think of themselves as having any concern with one another: Tom Robertson, Ibsen, Pinero, and Barrie might as well have belonged to a different solar system as far as Irving was concerned; and the same was true of their respective predecessors.
Thus was established an evil tradition; but I at least can plead that it does not always hold good. If Forbes Robertson had not been there to play Caesar, I should not have written *Caesar and Cleopatra*. If Ellen Terry had never been born, *Captain Brassbound’s Conversion* would never have been effected. *The Devil’s Disciple*, with which I won my *cordon bleu* in America as a potboiler, would have had a different sort of hero if Richard Mansfield had been a different sort of actor, though the actual commission to write it came from an English actor, William Terriss, who was assassinated before he recovered from the dismay into which the result of his rash proposal threw him. For it must be said that the actor or actress who inspires or commissions a play as often as not regards it as a Frankenstein’s monster, and will have none of it.

===Chinese===

还应看到：伟大的戏比伟大的演员活得长，虽然蹩脚的戏远不如它们最蹩脚的扮演者活得长。结果是，伟大的演员不再逼同时代作者供他英雄角色，而是退回莎士比亚的保留剧目，从一只死手里拿他需要的东西。十九世纪，基恩、麦克雷迪、巴里·沙利文和欧文们的生涯，本该产出一批强度堪比埃斯库罗斯、索福克勒斯、欧里庇得斯的英雄剧；却什么也没产出：这些演员演的是死人的作品，或者偶尔演几位算不上正规职业剧作家的在世诗人。谢里丹·诺尔斯、布尔沃·利顿、威尔斯和丁尼生，为当时的伟大演员造过几匹光芒刺目的人造高头马；可真正支撑着戏院、也被戏院支撑着的正牌剧作家们，并不伺候大演员：他们竞争不起一位“不属于一代而属于万世”的诗人，何况这位诗人对演员兼经理们还有一重压倒性的吸引力：不收版税。结果是剧作家同大演员从此互不相认：就欧文而论，汤姆·罗伯森、易卜生、皮尼罗、巴里，同另一个太阳系里的居民也差不了多少；他们的前辈彼此之间，也一样。
一个坏传统就这样立了起来；可至少我可以申明，它并不总是灵验。若不是有福布斯·罗伯森在那儿演凯撒，我不会写《凯撒与克莉奥佩特拉》。若不是埃伦·泰里降生人世，《布拉斯邦德上尉的转变》根本无从转变。《魔鬼的门徒》——我靠它在美国挣得快煮书的一等勋章——倘若理查德·曼斯菲尔德是另一种演员，它的英雄也会是另一种；尽管实际的写作委托来自一位英国演员，威廉·特里斯，他还没从他那鲁莽提议的后果给他的惊愕中缓过来，就遇刺身亡了。因为不得不说明：激发或委托一出戏的那位演员或女演员，十有八九把这出戏看作弗兰肯斯泰因的怪物，拒不认账。

===Original===

That does not make him or her any the less parental in the fecundity of the playwright.
To an author who has any feeling of his business there is a keen and whimsical joy in divining and revealing a side of an actor’s genius overlooked before, and unsuspected even by the actor himself. When I snatched Mr. Louis Calvert from Shakespeare, and made him wear a frock coat and silk hat on the stage for perhaps the first time in his life, I do not think he expected in the least that his performance would enable me to boast of his Tom Broadbent as a genuine stage classic. Mrs. Patrick Campbell was famous before I wrote for her, but not for playing illiterate cockney flower-maidens. And in the case which is provoking me to all these impertinences, I am quite sure that Miss Gertrude Kingston, who first made her reputation as an impersonator of the most delightfully feather-headed and inconsequent ingenues, thought me more than usually mad when I persuaded her to play the Helen of Euripides, and then launched her on a queenly career as Catherine of Russia.
It is not the whole truth that if we take care of the actors the plays will take care of themselves; nor is it any truer that if we take care of the plays the actors will take care of themselves. There is both give and take in the business. I have seen plays written for actors that made me exclaim, “How oft the sight of means to do ill deeds makes deeds ill done!” But Burbage may have flourished the prompt copy of *Hamlet* under Shakespeare’s nose at the tenth rehearsal and cried, “How oft the sight of means to do great deeds makes playwrights great!” I say the tenth because I am convinced that at the first he denounced his part as a rotten one; thought the ghost’s speech ridiculously long; and wanted to play the king. Anyhow, whether he had the wit to utter it or not, the boast would have been a valid one. The best conclusion is that every actor should say, “If I create the hero in myself, God will send an author to write his part.” For in the long run the actors will get the authors, and the authors the actors, they deserve.

===Chinese===

这并不减损他或她在剧作家多产一事上的父母身份。
对一个对自己的行当还有感情的作者来说，揣摩并揭示一位演员天才中从前被忽略、连演员自己也未曾疑心的一面，有一种尖锐而古怪的快乐。当我把路易斯·卡尔弗特先生从莎士比亚那里抢过来，让他生平头一遭在台上穿长礼服、戴丝帽时，我想他万万没有料到，他的表演会使我敢夸口：他的汤姆·布罗德本特是一尊真正的舞台经典。帕特里克·坎贝尔夫人在我为她写戏之前就出了名，可不是以扮演目不识丁的伦敦土腔卖花女出的名。而在眼下惹出我这一通冒失话的这桩案子里，我可以拿准：格特鲁德·金斯顿小姐——她最初的声名，是扮演那些最叫人喜爱的没头脑、无逻辑的少女赚来的——被我劝去演欧里庇得斯的海伦，继而把她推上俄国凯瑟琳的女王生涯时，一定觉得我比平常更疯。
“只消照看好演员，戏自会照看好自己”，这不是全部的真理；“只消照看好戏，演员自会照看好自己”，也未必更真。这行当里向来有来有往。我见过为演员写的戏，叫我失声喊出：“啊，行恶的手段一旦在眼前，恶事何其容易办！”可伯比奇也可能在第十次排练时，把《哈姆雷特》的提词本在莎士比亚鼻子底下挥着喊：“啊，行大业的手段一旦在眼前，剧作家何其容易成大器！”我说第十次，因为我坚信头一次他准把他那个角色骂成一文不值；嫌鬼魂的台词长得荒唐；还吵着要演国王。总之，不论他有没有急智说出口，这句大话都站得住。最好的结论是：每个演员都该说：“只要我在自己身上造出英雄来，上帝自会派一位作者来写他的戏。”因为归根结底，演员得到的正是他们应得的作者，作者得到的也正是应得的演员。

===Original===

1776. **Patiomkin** in his bureau in the Winter Palace, St. Petersburg. Huge palatial apartment: style, Russia in the eighteenth century imitating the *Versailles du Roi Soleil*. Extravagant luxury. Also dirt and disorder.
**Patiomkin**, gigantic in stature and build, his face marred by the loss of one eye and a marked squint in the other, sits at the end of a table littered with papers and the remains of three or four successive breakfasts. He has supplies of coffee and brandy at hand sufficient for a party of ten. His coat, encrusted with diamonds, is on the floor. It has fallen off a chair placed near the other end of the table for the convenience of visitors. His court sword, with its attachments, is on the chair. His three-cornered hat, also bejewelled, is on the table. He himself is half dressed in an unfastened shirt and an immense dressing gown, once gorgeous, now food-splashed and dirty, as it serves him for towel, handkerchief, duster, and every other use to which a textile fabric can be put by a slovenly man. It does not conceal his huge hairy chest, nor his half-buttoned knee breeches, nor his legs. These are partly clad in silk stockings, which he occasionally hitches up to his knees, and presently shakes down to his shins, by his restless movement. His feet are thrust into enormous slippers, worth, with their crust of jewels, several thousand roubles apiece.
Superficially **Patiomkin** is a violent, brutal barbarian, an upstart despot of the most intolerable and dangerous type, ugly, lazy, and disgusting in his personal habits. Yet ambassadors report him the ablest man in Russia, and the one who can do most with the still abler Empress Catherine II, who is not a Russian but a German, by no means barbarous or intemperate in her personal habits. She not only disputes with Frederick the Great the reputation of being the cleverest monarch in Europe, but may even put in a very plausible claim to be the cleverest and most attractive individual alive. Now she not only tolerates **Patiomkin** long after she has got over her first romantic attachment to him, but esteems him highly as a counsellor and a good friend. His love letters are among the best on record. He has a wild sense of humor, which enables him to laugh at himself as well as at everybody else.

===Chinese===

1776年。圣彼得堡，冬宫里**帕乔姆金**的办公室。宏大的宫殿厅堂：风格是十八世纪的俄国模仿“太阳王的凡尔赛”。奢华无度。同时也肨脏杂乱。
**帕乔姆金**，身量魁梧奇伟，脸坏了一只眼，另一只明显斜视，坐在一张长桌的尽头；桌上摊满文件，和三四顿接连的早餐的残迹。他手边的咖啡和白兰地，足够十个人的宴会用。他那件缀满钻石的外衣掉在地板上——是从桌子另一头、为访客方便放的那把椅子上滑下去的。他那柄朝服剑，连着配挂，在椅子上。他那顶三角帽，同样珠光宝气，在桌上。他本人衣冠半敞：一件没系扣的衬衫，一件一度华贵、如今沾满饭渍的肥大晨袍——因为它兼作他的毛巾、手帕、拂尘，和一切懒汉能使布料的用途。晨袍遮不住他毛茸茸的宽阔胸膛，遮不住扣了一半的及膝短裤，也遮不住双腿。两条腿半套着丝袜；他时不时把丝袜拽到膝盖，又随着不停的扭动滑回小腿。两只脚插在一双巨大的拖鞋里——那上面的珠宝皮壳，一双值好几千卢布。
表面上，**帕乔姆金**是个凶暴蛮横的野人，一个最叫人受不了、最危险的下克上暴发僭主，丑陋、懒惰、个人习气令人作呕。可大使们回报说他是俄国最有能耐的人，也是最能同那位更有能耐的女皇凯瑟琳二世打交道的人——女皇不是俄国人，是德国人，个人习气一点也不野蛮纵酒。她不但同腓特烈大帝争夺欧洲最聪明君主的声名，甚至很有几分道理，可算当时在世最聪明、最可喜的个人。如今她不但容忍**帕乔姆金**——她对早年的那段热恋早已过去——还十分器重他这位谋臣和好友。他的情书是有史以来最好的几批。他有一种狂放的幽默感，叫他笑得动自己，也笑得动旁人。

===Original===

In the eyes of the English visitor now about to be admitted to his presence he may be an outrageous ruffian. In fact he actually is an outrageous ruffian, in no matter whose eyes; but the visitor will find out, as everyone else sooner or later fends out, that he is a man to be reckoned with even by those who are not intimidated by his temper, bodily strength, and exalted rank.
A pretty young lady, **Varinka**, his favorite niece, is lounging on an ottoman between his end of the table and the door, very sulky and dissatisfied, perhaps because he is preoccupied with his papers and his brandy bottle, and she can see nothing of him but his broad back.
There is a screen behind the ottoman.
*An old soldier, a **Cossack sergeant**, enters.*
The Sergeant
*Softly to the lady, holding the door handle.* Little darling honey: is his Highness the prince very busy?
Varinka
His Highness the prince is very busy. He is singing out of tune; he is biting his nails; he is scratching his head; he is hitching up his untidy stockings; he is making himself disgusting and odious to everybody; and he is pretending to read state papers that he does not understand because he is too lazy and selfish to talk and be companionable.
Patiomkin
*Growls; then wipes his nose with his dressing gown.* !!
Varinka
Pig. Ugh! *She curls herself up with a shiver of disgust and retires from the conversation.*
The Sergeant
*Stealing across to the coat, and picking it up to replace it on the back of the chair.* Little Father, the English captain, so highly recommended to you by old Fritz of Prussia, by the English ambassador, and by Monsieur Voltaire (whom *crossing himself* may God in his infinite mercy damn eternally!), is in the antechamber and desires audience.
Patiomkin
*Deliberately.* To hell with the English captain; and to hell with old Fritz of Prussia; and to hell with the English ambassador; and to hell with Monsieur Voltaire; and to hell with you too!
The Sergeant
Have mercy on me, Little Father. Your head is bad this morning. You drink too much French brandy and too little good Russian kvass.
Patiomkin
*With sudden fury.* Why are visitors of consequence announced by a sergeant? *Springing at him and seizing him by the throat.* What do you mean by this, you hound? Do you want five thousand blows of the stick? Where is General Volkonsky?
The Sergeant
*On his knees.

Patiomkin
I don’t want to know who you are. What do you want?
Edstaston
An audience of the Empress. ***Patiomkin** contemptuously throws the letter aside. **Edstaston** adds hotly.* Also some civility, if you please.
Patiomkin
*With derision.* Ho!
Varinka
My uncle is receiving you with unusual civility, Captain. He has just kicked a general downstairs.
Edstaston
A Russian general, madam?
Varinka
Of course.
Edstaston
I must allow myself to say, madam, that your uncle had better not attempt to kick an English officer downstairs.
Patiomkin
You want me to kick you upstairs: eh? You want an audience of the Empress.
Edstaston
I have said nothing about kicking, sir. If it comes to that, my boots shall speak for me. Her Majesty has signified a desire to have news of the rebellion in America. I have served against the rebels; and I am instructed to place myself at the disposal of her Majesty, and to describe the events of the war to her as an eyewitness, in a discreet and agreeable manner.
Patiomkin
Psha! I know. You think if she once sets eyes on your face and your uniform your fortune is made. You think that if she could stand a man like me, with only one eye, and a cross eye at that, she must fall down at your feet at first sight, eh?
Edstaston
*Shocked and indignant.* I think nothing of the sort; and I’ll trouble you not to repeat it. If I were a Russian subject and you made such a boast about my queen, I’d strike you across the face with my sword. ***Patiomkin**, with a yell of fury, rushes at him.* Hands off, you swine!

===Chinese===

上帝知道，他需要您的恩典和庇——*（他见**帕乔姆金**要拿瓶子砸他，一溜烟不见了。**上尉**望着这些前奏，又是惊讶又是不快；而**帕乔姆金**几乎不屑看来客一眼——却仍用那只独眼的余角把他打量了个透——粗声粗气一个字。*怎么样？

*（扯开封皮，扫了约莫一秒钟。）*你要什么？

上尉，我叔叔这已经是格外客气地接待您了。他刚刚才把一位将军踢下楼。

俄国将军吗，夫人？
瓦琳卡
当然。
埃德斯塔斯顿
恕我冒昧，夫人，令叔最好别想也把一位英国军官踢下楼。

你是要我把你踢*上*楼：嗯？你要觐见女皇。

我谁也没说要踢，先生。真要闹到那一步，我的靴子会替我说话。陛下已表示希望了解美洲叛乱的近况。我打过叛军；我奉命听候陛下差遣，以目击者的身份、用审慎而可喜的方式向她讲述战事。
帕乔姆金
啐！我知道。你以为她只要看上你的脸和你的军服一眼，你的前程就定了。你以为她既然受得了我这样的男人——独眼，还是斜眼——见你第一眼就必定拜倒在你的脚下，嗯？

*（又惊又怒。）*我没有这种想法；请你别再说一遍。我若是俄国臣民，你敢这样说我家女王，我一剑抽在你脸上。*（**帕乔姆金**怒吼一声，扑向他。）*把手拿开，你这猪猡！

*As **Patiomkin**, towering over him, attempts to seize him by the throat, **Edstaston**, who is a bit of a wrestler, adroitly backheels him. He falls, amazed, on his back.*

*Rushing out.* Help! Call the guard! The Englishman is murdering my uncle! Help! Help!

Little Father﻿—

*Roaring.* Get out. Get out, all of you. *They withdraw, much relieved at their escape from the pistol. **Patiomkin** attempts to rise, and rolls over.* Here! help me up, will you? Don’t you see that I’m drunk and can’t get up?

*Suspiciously.* You want to get hold of me.

*Squatting resignedly against the chair on which his clothes hang.* Very well, then: I shall stay where I am, because I’m drunk and you’re afraid of me.

*Ecstatically.* Darling: your lips are the gates of truth. Invalided home from America at the request of Aunt Fanny, Lady-in-Waiting to the Queen. All right, eh?

*Flapping his fingers at him grotesquely.* Only one eye, darling. Cross eye. Sees everything. Read lerrer ince﻿—ince﻿—istastaneously. Kindly give me vinegar borle. Green borle. On’y to sober me. Too drunk to speak proply. If you would be so kind, darling. Green borle.

===Original===

***Edstaston**, still suspicious, shakes his head and keeps his pistols ready.* Reach it myself. *He reaches behind him up to the table, and snatches at the green bottle, from which he takes a copious draught. *Delicately.* The other side, your Highness.

Get out.

Edstaston
Certainly. I am a Bachelor of Arts.
Patiomkin

In real life, darling, all facts are unpleasant. *Greatly pleased with himself.* Another epigram! Then, recollecting himself.* But I have not asked you to sit down. *He rises and goes to the other chair.* I am a savage: a barbarian. *He throws the shirt and coat over the table on to the floor and puts his sword on the table.* Be seated, Captain.

Thank you.

*Resuming his seat.* By the way, what was the piece of advice I was going to give you?

As you did not give it, I don’t know. Allow me to add that I have not asked for your advice.

I give it to you unasked, delightful Englishman. I remember it now. It was this. Don’t try to become Tsar of Russia.

*In astonishment.* I haven’t the slightest intention﻿—

Not now; but you will have: take my word for it. It will strike you as a splendid idea to have conscientious scruples﻿—to desire the blessing of the Church on your union with Catherine.

*Racing in utter amazement.* My union with Catherine! You’re mad.

*Shortly: sitting down again.* I do not wish to discuss it.

You think she murdered him?

你是单身汉就够了，亲爱的：“文艺”凯瑟琳自会供应。啊哈！又是一句隽语！我今天在兴头上。
埃德斯塔斯顿
*（厧尬又有点着恼。）*我得请殿下换个话题。作为俄罗斯的宾客，我是女皇的客人；我直说吧：我既无权利、也无兴致拿陛下调侃。
帕乔姆金
你有良心上的顾忌？
埃德斯塔斯顿
我有绅士的顾忌。
帕乔姆金
在俄罗斯，绅士没有顾忌。在俄罗斯，我们面对事实。
埃德斯塔斯顿
在英国，先生，事实若是不愉快的事实，绅士从不面对。
帕乔姆金
在实际生活里，亲爱的，一切事实都不愉快。*（大为得意。）*又是一句隽语！我那可恶的书记官死哪儿去了？这些宝石该记下来传给后世。*（他冲到桌边；坐下；抓起笔。随即又想起。）*可我还没请你坐呢。*（他起身走向另一把椅子。）*我是野人：是蛮子。*（他把衬衫和外衣扔过桌面掃到地上，把剑放到桌上。）*请坐，上尉。
埃德斯塔斯顿
谢谢。
*（两人彬彬有礼地对弯。**帕乔姆金**那股古怪夸张的劲头害他失了平衡，几乎跌在**埃德斯塔斯顿**身上；后者扶住他，接过让出的椅子。）*
帕乔姆金
*（回到座位。）*对了，我方才要给你的忠告是什么来着？
埃德斯塔斯顿
您没给，我不知道。恕我加一句：我并没有请教您的忠告。
帕乔姆金
不请教我也送你，可爱的英国人。我想起来了。是这样：别想当俄国的沙皇。
埃德斯塔斯顿
*（愕然。）*我丝毫没有这个意思——
帕乔姆金
现在没有；往后会有：信我的话。到那时你会觉得，来一点良心上的顾忌——求教会祝福你同凯瑟琳的结合——是个绝妙的主意。
埃德斯塔斯顿
*（惊得跳起来。）*我同凯瑟琳的结合！你疯了。
帕乔姆金
*（无动于衷。）*你哪天漏出这个意思，哪天就是你的垮台。再说，当凯瑟琳的丈夫不吉利。彼得的下场你知道吧？
埃德斯塔斯顿
*（生硬地；重新坐下。）*我不愿谈论这件事。
帕乔姆金
你以为是她杀了他？

===Original===

Edstaston
I know that people have said so.
Patiomkin
*Thunderously; springing to his feet.* It is a lie: Orloff murdered him. *Subsiding a little.* He also knocked my eye out; but *sitting down placidly* I succeeded him for all that. And *patting **Edstaston’s** hand very affectionately* I’m sorry to say, darling, that if you become Tsar, I shall murder you.
Edstaston
*Ironically returning the caress.* Thank you. The occasion will not arise. *Rising.* I have the honor to wish your Highness good morning.
Patiomkin
*Jumping up and stopping him on his way to the door.* Tut tut! I’m going to take you to the Empress now, this very instant.
Edstaston
In these boots? Impossible! I must change.
Patiomkin
Nonsense! You shall come just as you are. You shall show her your calves later on.
Edstaston
But it will take me only half an hour to﻿—
Patiomkin
In half an hour it will be too late for the *petit lever*. Come along. Damn it, man, I must oblige the British ambassador, and the French ambassador, and old Fritz, and Monsieur Voltaire and the rest of them. *He shouts rudely to the door.* Varinka! *To **Edstaston**, with tears in his voice.* Varinka shall persuade you: nobody can refuse Varinka anything. My niece. A treasure, I assure you. Beautiful! devoted! fascinating! *Shouting again.* Varinka: where the devil are you?
Varinka
*Returning.* I’ll not be shouted for. You have the voice of a bear, and the manners of a tinker.
Patiomkin
Tsh‑sh‑sh. Little angel Mother: you must behave yourself before the English captain. *He takes off his dressing gown and throws it over the papers and the breakfasts; picks up his coat; and disappears behind the screen to complete his toilette.*
Edstaston
Madam! *He bows.*
Varinka
*Curtseying.*
*Monsieur le Capitaine!*
Edstaston
I must apologize for the disturbance I made, madam.
Patiomkin
*Behind the screen.* You must not call her madam. You must call her Little Mother, and beautiful darling.
Edstaston
My respect for the lady will not permit it.
Varinka
Respect! How can you respect the niece of a savage?
Edstaston
*Deprecating.* Oh, madam!
Varinka
Heaven is my witness, Little English Father, we need someone who is not afraid of him. He is so strong! I hope you will throw him down on the floor many, many, many times.
Patiomkin
*Behind the screen.* Varinka!
Varinka
Yes?

埃德斯塔斯顿
我知道有人这样说过。

*（雷霆般；跳起来。）*那是谎话：是奥尔洛夫杀的。*（稍稍平息。）*他还打瞎了我一只眼；不过*（安然坐下）*我还是接替了他。还有*（深情地拍拍**埃德斯塔斯顿**的手）*很遗憾，亲爱的，你若当了沙皇，我就得杀你。

*（跳起来，拦住他去门的路。）*嗬嗬！我这就带你去见女皇，此时此刻。

穿这双靴子？不可能！我得换装。

胡说！就这样来。你那两条小腿，回头再给她看。

瓦琳卡
*（回来。）*不许人喊我。您的嗓音像熊，规矩像补锅匠。
帕乔姆金
嘫嘫嘫。小天使妈妈：在英国上尉面前要有规矩。*（他脱下晨袍，扔在文件和早餐上；抓起外衣；进屏风后头去完成他的穿戴。）*
埃德斯塔斯顿
夫人！*（一躬。）*
瓦琳卡
*（屈膝礼。）*
上尉先生！
埃德斯塔斯顿
夫人，方才的骚乱，我得道歉。
帕乔姆金
*（屏风后。）*不许叫她夫人。要叫她小妈妈，美丽的亲亲。
埃德斯塔斯顿
我对这位女士的敬意不容我这样叫。
瓦琳卡
敬意！一个野人的侄女，您怎么敬得起来？
埃德斯塔斯顿
*（不以为然。）*哦，夫人！
瓦琳卡
老天作证，英国小爸爸，我们需要一个不怕他的人。他力气多大呀！我希望您把他摔倒在地上，许多次，许多次，许多次。
帕乔姆金
*（屏风后。）*瓦琳卡！
瓦琳卡
嗯？

===Original===

Patiomkin
Go and look through the keyhole of the Imperial bedchamber; and bring me word whether the Empress is awake yet.
Varinka
*Fi donc!* I do not look through keyholes.
Patiomkin
*Emerging, having arranged his shirt and put on his diamonded coat.* You have been badly brought up, little darling. Would any lady or gentleman walk unannounced into a room without first looking through the keyhole? *Taking his sword from the table and putting it on.* The great thing in life is to be simple; and the perfectly simple thing is to look through keyholes. Another epigram: the fifth this morning! Where is my fool of a chancellor? Where is Popof?
Edstaston
*Choking with suppressed laughter.* !!!!
Patiomkin
*Gratified.* Darling, you appreciate my epigram.
Edstaston
Excuse me. Pop off! Ha! ha! I can’t help laughing. What’s his real name, by the way, in case I meet him?
Varinka
*Surprised.* His real name? Popof, of course. Why do you laugh, Little Father?
Edstaston
How can anyone with a sense of humor help laughing? Pop off! *He is convulsed.*
Varinka
*Looking at her uncle, taps her forehead significantly.* !!
Patiomkin
*Aside to **Varinka**.* No: only English. He will amuse Catherine. *To **Edstaston**.* Come, you shall tell the joke to the Empress: she is by way of being a humorist. *He takes him by the arm, and leads him towards the door.*
Edstaston
*Resisting.* No, really. I am not fit﻿—
Patiomkin
Persuade him, Little angel Mother.
Varinka
*Taking his other arm.* Yes, yes, yes. Little English Father: God knows it is your duty to be brave and wait on the Empress. Come.
Edstaston
No. I had rather﻿—
Patiomkin
*Hauling him along.* Come.
Varinka
*Pulling him and coaxing him.* Come, little love: you can’t refuse me.
Edstaston
But how can I?
Patiomkin
Why not? She won’t eat you.
Varinka
She will; but you must come.
Edstaston
I assure you﻿—it is quite out of the question﻿—my clothes﻿—
Varinka
You look perfect.
Patiomkin
Come along, darling.
Edstaston
*Struggling.* Impossible﻿—
Varinka
Come, come, come.
Edstaston
No. Believe me﻿—I don’t wish﻿—I﻿—
Varinka
Carry him, uncle.
Patiomkin
*Lifting him in his arms like a father carrying a little boy.* Yes: I’ll carry you.
Edstaston
Dash it all, this is ridiculous!
Varinka
*Seizing his ankles and dancing as he is carried out.* You must come. If you kick you will blacken my eyes.
Patiomkin
Come, baby, come.

帕乔姆金
去看看寝宫的锁眼；回来告诉我女皇醒了没有。
瓦琳卡
啐！我不看锁眼。
帕乔姆金
*（穿戴齐整地出来：衬衫理好，缀钻石的外衣上身。）*你的教养太差了，小亲亲。哪有淑女绅士不先看锁眼、不打招呼就进屋的？*（从桌上拿起剑佩上。）*人生头一件大事是简单；而最简单不过的事，就是看锁眼。又是一句隽语：今儿早上第五句！我那傻瓜书记官呢？波波夫呢？
埃德斯塔斯顿
*（忍笑忍得透不过气。）*！！！！
帕乔姆金
*（受用。）*亲爱的，你赏识我的隽语。

恕我。波波夫走开！哈！哈！忍不住。顺便问一句，万一遇上，他的真名叫什么？
瓦琳卡
*（诧异。）*真名？当然叫波波夫。您笑什么，英国小爸爸？
埃德斯塔斯顿
有点幽默感的人怎么会不笑？波波夫走开！*（他笑得直不起腰。）*
瓦琳卡
*（看看叔叔，意味深长地敲敲自己的额头。）*！！
帕乔姆金
*（旁白，对**瓦琳卡**。）*不：只是英国人。他会逗凯瑟琳笑。*（对**埃德斯塔斯顿**。）*来，这个笑话你去讲给女皇听：她勉强算个幽默家。*（他拈住他的胳膊，往门口带。）*
埃德斯塔斯顿
*（抗拒。）*不，真的。我不配——
帕乔姆金
劝劝他，小天使妈妈。
瓦琳卡
*（拈住他另一条胳膊。）*是，是，是。英国小爸爸：上帝知道，勇敢侍奉女皇是您的本分。来。
埃德斯塔斯顿
不。我宁可——
帕乔姆金
*（拖着他走。）*来。
瓦琳卡
*（又拉又哄。）*来嘛，小亲亲：你可拒不了我。

可我怎么能？

她会吃；可你也得来。

您这样好看极了。
帕乔姆金
走吧，亲爱的。
埃德斯塔斯顿

瓦琳卡
来，来，来。

叔叔，抱起他来。

*（像父亲抱小男孩那样把他抱进怀里。）*好：我抱你。
埃德斯塔斯顿
搞什么名堂，这太荒唐了！
瓦琳卡
*（拈住他的脚腕，在他被抱出门时跳着舞步。）*您必须来。踢腾的话会打青我的眼睛。

来，宝宝，来。
